standard_text: Use the properties of operations, particularly the distributive property, leading to products such as (-1)(-1) = 1 and the rules for multiplying signed numbers.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to multiply signed rational numbers, justify the sign rules from the properties of operations, and apply the distributive property with signed factors. The on-grade work moves from the number line model of a negative times a positive, through the sign rules and signed integer products, to products of signed fractions and decimals and distributing a signed factor to every term inside parentheses. The sign rule itself is quick to teach; what actually sinks students is the size arithmetic, most often weak multiplication facts and shaky fraction and decimal multiplication. Intervention should first secure grade 3 facts and grade 5 decimal times whole number products, then rebuild grade 6 fraction and decimal multiplication, and only then attach the signs.

steps.rationale: The standard's concrete entry (Below proficiency): a negative times a positive is repeated jumps left on a number line, so the product is negative. This grounds sign in a picture before it becomes a rule.

The standard's headline -- 'the rules for multiplying signed numbers,' anchored by (-1)(-1) = 1. Deciding a product's sign by counting negative factors is separable from computing its size, so it is taught on its own.
The Approaching-proficiency demand: multiply two or more signed integers by applying the sign rule to the count of negatives and multiplication facts to the size.

The At-proficiency computational core: extend signed multiplication to non-integer rationals -- fractions, mixed numbers, and decimals -- where the sign rule is unchanged but the magnitude arithmetic is harder.
The At-proficiency application named in the standard: use the distributive property to simplify an expression like -1/2(9 + 3), distributing the signed factor to every term.

The Above-proficiency synthesis: identify and create equivalent products using the properties of operations and the sign rules, recognizing that moving a negative preserves the value while a second negative flips it.

skills.name: Recall multiplication facts using arrays

prerequisite_skill.description: Recall products of whole numbers through 12 x 12, rebuilding a stuck fact from an array or a friendly fact.

skills.i_do_script: A multiplication fact is an array: 6 x 4 is 6 rows of 4 dots, 24 dots in all. When a fact is stuck, I rebuild it from one I own. Watch: 7 x 8. I know 7 x 5 is 35, and I need 3 more rows of 7, which is 21 more, so 7 x 8 is 56. The array shows why that works: I split the 8 columns into 5 and 3. Every signed product later needs these facts for the size of the answer, and the calculator is not allowed.

canonical_error.pattern: Mis-recalls a basic fact, often landing on a neighboring product
canonical_error.example: Says 7 x 8 = 54, mixing it up with 6 x 9, instead of 56
canonical_error.why: The fact is not automatic, so the student guesses from memory and lands on a nearby product. The array splits the fact into pieces the student can rebuild and check.

skills.item_template: A single whole-number multiplication fact through 12 x 12. Short response fluency bank, no calculator.

skills.name: Multiply a decimal by a whole number

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiply a decimal to the hundredths by a one-digit whole number, using money or a grid to place the decimal point.

skills.i_do_script: Multiplying a decimal by a whole number is repeated groups of a decimal amount. Watch: 0.3 x 4 means 4 groups of 3 tenths. Count the tenths: 3, 6, 9, 12 tenths, and 12 tenths is 1.2. In money, 4 groups of 30 cents is 120 cents, which is 1 dollar 20 cents. The shortcut is multiply 3 x 4 = 12, then remember I was counting tenths, so the answer is 1.2, not 12. The decimal point is not decoration; it says what size unit I counted.

canonical_error.pattern: Ignores the decimal point and treats the decimal like a whole number
canonical_error.why: The student multiplies the digits and forgets the factor was tenths, not ones. Four groups of 3 tenths is 12 tenths, and 12 tenths regroups to 1.2. Money makes it visible: 30 cents four times cannot be 12 dollars.

skills.item_template: A decimal to the hundredths times a one-digit whole number. Clean numbers, short response fluency bank, no calculator.

redirect_script.praise: You kept track of the unit, so the decimal point landed where it belongs.

vocabulary.definition: The first place to the right of the decimal point; 0.3 is 3 tenths.

skills.name: Multiply positive fractions using an area model

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiply a fraction by a fraction or a whole number, seeing the product as a part of a part on an area model.

skills.i_do_script: A fraction times a fraction asks for a part OF a part. Watch 2/3 x 3/4: I shade 3/4 of a square with vertical stripes, then take 2/3 of that shaded part with horizontal stripes. The square is now cut into 12 small pieces and the double-shaded part covers 6 of them, so 2/3 x 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2. The rule the picture proves: multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms. For a whole number, write it over 1: 3/4 x 8 = 3/4 x 8/1 = 24/4 = 6, which is just 3/4 OF 8.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the fractions instead of taking a part of a part
canonical_error.why: The student falls back on the addition routine because it is more practiced. The area model shows the product is a piece OF a piece, smaller than either factor, not the two amounts pushed together.

skills.item_template: A product of two positive fractions, or a fraction times a whole number (denominators up to 12). Numeric response, no calculator.

sample_items.stem: Which product does an area model show for 1/2 of 4/5?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1/2 x 4/5 = 4/10 = 2/5. Adding tops and bottoms gives 5/7; forgetting to take the half leaves 4/5.

redirect_script.stop: Is this a part OF a part, or two amounts joined together?
redirect_script.prompt: Draw the square: shade 3/4 one way, then take 2/3 of the shaded part the other way. Count the double-shaded pieces over the total pieces. That is top times top over bottom times bottom.
redirect_script.praise: You took a part of a part, and the picture matched the rule.

vocabulary.definition: A square cut both ways to show a fraction of a fraction; the double-shaded part is the product.
In fraction multiplication, 'of' means times: 2/3 of 3/4 is 2/3 x 3/4.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a square. Cut it into 4 vertical strips and shade 3 of them for 3/4.
Now we need 2/3 OF that shaded part. How should we cut the square the other way?
Cut it into 3 horizontal strips and shade 2 of them across. The square now has 12 pieces, and 6 are double-shaded: 2/3 x 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2. Top times top, bottom times bottom.
If a student says 5/7 or 17/12, they added. Ask: is 2/3 OF 3/4 bigger or smaller than 3/4? The picture says smaller.
Your turn: draw the area model for 1/2 x 4/5.

practice_problems.answer: He added the fractions instead of multiplying. Half OF a third is a smaller piece: 1/2 x 1/3 = 1/6.

activities.instructions:

skills.name: Multiply positive decimals

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiply two positive decimals, placing the decimal point by counting decimal places or by reasoning about size.

skills.i_do_script: 0.4 x 0.3 asks for 4 tenths OF 3 tenths, a part of a part, just like fractions. Watch on a hundredths grid: shade 3 tenths one way, 4 tenths the other way, and the overlap covers 12 of the 100 small squares, so 0.4 x 0.3 = 0.12. The shortcut agrees: 4 x 3 = 12, and tenths times tenths makes hundredths, one decimal place plus one decimal place is two decimal places, so 0.12. Always sanity check the size: both factors are less than 1, so the product must be smaller than either factor.

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies the digits correctly but misplaces the decimal point
canonical_error.example: Writes 0.4 x 0.3 = 1.2 (one decimal place) instead of 0.12
canonical_error.why: The student copies one decimal place from the factors instead of adding the places. Tenths times tenths makes hundredths, and the grid shows the overlap is 12 small squares, not more than a whole.

skills.item_template: A product of two positive decimals to the hundredths (digit products stay in fact range). Numeric response, no calculator.

sample_items.stem: Which is the product of 2.5 x 1.2?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 25 x 12 = 300 with two decimal places gives 3.00. Misplacing the point gives 30 or 0.3; adding gives 3.7.

redirect_script.stop: How many decimal places should the answer have?
redirect_script.prompt: Multiply the digits as whole numbers first. Then add the decimal places in the two factors and count that many places back in. Check the size: a number less than 1 makes the other factor smaller, not bigger.
redirect_script.praise: You counted the places and checked the size, so the point landed where it belongs.

vocabulary.definition: A position to the right of the decimal point: tenths, then hundredths.
The second place to the right of the decimal point; tenths times tenths makes hundredths.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a hundredths grid. Shade 3 columns (0.3) in one color, then shade 4 rows (0.4) in another.
How many small squares are shaded both ways? What is each small square worth?
The overlap is 4 rows of 3 squares, 12 squares, and each is one hundredth: 0.4 x 0.3 = 0.12. The shortcut matches: 4 x 3 = 12 with two decimal places.
If a student writes 1.2, ask: both factors are less than 1, so can the product be more than 1? Look at the overlap.
Your turn: use the grid or the place count to find 0.6 x 0.5.

skills.name: Model the product of a negative and a positive on a number line
skills.i_do_script: Multiplying is repeated jumps, and the direction of the jumps sets the sign. Watch a number line with 3 equal jumps of 2 units to the LEFT, starting at 0 and ending at -6. Each jump to the left is -2, repeated 3 times, so this models -2 x 3 = -6. Jumps to the left make a negative product; the landing point IS the product.

canonical_error.pattern: Ignores the direction (sign) of the jumps and models it as a positive product
canonical_error.example: For 3 jumps of 2 to the LEFT (ending at -6), writes 2 x 3 instead of -2 x 3
canonical_error.why: The student counts the size of the jumps but not their leftward direction. A jump to the left is a negative amount, so the factor must carry a negative sign.

skills.item_template: A number-line model of repeated jumps (one factor negative); student picks the matching expression and product. MC/short response.

sample_items.stem: A number line shows 3 jumps of 2 units to the LEFT, starting at 0 and ending at -6. Which expression does it model?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Left jumps are negative: -2 x 3 = -6. Dropping the sign gives 2 x 3; making both negative gives a positive product.

vocabulary.definition: Numbers with a positive or negative sign; left of zero is negative.

skills.name: Determine the sign of a product by counting negative factors
skills.i_do_script: Nobody has to take 'a negative times a negative is positive' on faith -- the pattern proves it. Watch this column: 3 x (-4) = -12, 2 x (-4) = -8, 1 x (-4) = -4, 0 x (-4) = 0. Every time the first factor drops by 1, the answer climbs by 4. Keep the pattern going past zero: (-1) x (-4) must be +4, and (-2) x (-4) must be +8. The distributive property says the same thing: (-4)(-1 + 1) = (-4)(0) = 0, and distributing gives (-4)(-1) + (-4) = 0, so (-4)(-1) has to be +4 to cancel the -4. THAT is why two negatives make a positive. Once the why is settled, the shortcut is counting: the sign of a product depends only on how many negative factors there are -- even count means positive, odd count means negative. (-2)(-5) has two negatives (even): positive. (-2)(-5)(-1) has three (odd): negative.

skills.name: Identify and create equivalent signed products using properties of operations
skills.i_do_script: Two expressions are equivalent when they name the same product. A key move: a single negative sign can move from one factor to the other without changing the value, because a negative times a positive is still negative. Watch (-4/9)(3/4): its value is -1/3, and (4/9)(-3/4) is also -1/3 -- the negative just moved. But (-4/9)(-3/4) is NOT equivalent: adding a second negative makes it +1/3. canonical_error.why: The student treats every sign change as harmless. Moving ONE negative between factors preserves the value, but adding a SECOND negative flips the sign (odd vs even count of negatives).

skills.name: Apply the distributive property to simplify signed expressions
skills.i_do_script: Picture 9 + 3 as one bar made of a 9-piece and a 3-piece. Taking -1/2 of the bar means taking -1/2 of BOTH pieces -- skip a piece and you haven't taken half of the whole thing. The distributive property says a(b + c) = a x b + a x c -- the factor outside multiplies EVERY term inside, not just the first. Watch -1/2(9 + 3): multiply -1/2 x 9 = -4.5 AND -1/2 x 3 = -1.5, then add: -4.5 + (-1.5) = -6. I could also add inside first, 9 + 3 = 12, then -1/2 x 12 = -6 -- same answer. The trap is distributing to only the first term.

canonical_error.pattern: Distributes the outside factor to the first term only, leaving the second term unchanged
canonical_error.why: The student multiplies the first term and then just carries the second term along. The distributive property requires multiplying the outside factor by every term inside the parentheses.

skills.item_template: An expression a(b + c) with a signed rational factor; student distributes and simplifies. MC/numeric response.

sample_items.distractor_logic: -1/2 x 9 + -1/2 x 3 = -4.5 + (-1.5) = -6. Distributing to the first term only gives -1.5.

skills.name: Generalize the sign of a product using variables and inequalities
skills.i_do_script: You already know how to find the sign of a product by counting negative factors. Now the factors are letters, and you are told only which side of zero each one lives on. Watch: a < 0 and b > 0. I do not know what a and b are, and I do not need to. One factor is negative, one is positive, so exactly one negative goes into the product -- and one negative makes the product negative. So ab < 0, for every a and b that fit the description.

canonical_error.pattern: Distributes the sign of a variable across a sum, concluding that r(s + t) must be negative-times-positive term by term rather than finding the sign of the sum first
canonical_error.example: Given r < 0, s > 0, t > 0, says r(s + t) > 0 'because rs is negative and rt is negative and two negatives make a positive'
canonical_error.why: The student is applying the counting-negatives rule to terms that are being ADDED, not multiplied. The rule only governs factors. Inside the parentheses s + t is a single positive quantity, so r(s + t) is one negative times one positive.

skills.item_template: Variables with stated signs (a < 0, b > 0) and a claim about the sign or magnitude of a product or a product of a sum. Multiple choice, multi-select, or construct-an-inequality. No numeric answer exists; the reasoning is the answer.

sample_items.stem: Suppose a < 0 and b > 0. Which statement is true about the product ab?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Cannot be determined' tempts students who think they need actual values; ab > 0 comes from miscounting the negatives.

sample_items.stem: If r < 0, s > 0, and t > 0, select the three true statements: rs < 0, rt < 0, r(st) > 0, r(s + t) < 0, r(s + t) > 0, rst = 0.
sample_items.distractor_logic: r(st) > 0 miscounts one negative as two; r(s + t) > 0 is the distribute-the-sign error; rst = 0 imports the zero-product rule with nothing equal to zero.

sample_items.stem: m < 0 and n < 0. Is mn greater than, less than, or equal to zero? Write an inequality and justify it.
sample_items.answer: mn > 0. Two negative factors, and two negatives make a positive product.
sample_items.distractor_logic: mn < 0 counts the negatives but not the pairing.

sample_items.stem: p < 0 and q > 0, and |p| > |q|. What can you say about the sign of p + q, and about the sign of pq?
sample_items.answer: p + q < 0 because the negative has the larger magnitude; pq < 0 because exactly one factor is negative. Sign of a sum depends on magnitude; sign of a product does not.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Answering the same for both shows the sum rule and the product rule have collapsed into one.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- are those two things being multiplied, or added?

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: a < 0, b > 0. Underneath write ab, and leave a blank for the sign.
I have not told you what a and b are. Do you need to know, to decide the sign of ab?
How many of these two factors are negative? Count them out loud.
One negative factor. What does one negative do to a product?
If the student wants to pick values for a and b, let them -- then ask them to pick a DIFFERENT pair and check whether the sign changed. Two cases with the same sign is the argument.
New one: r < 0, s > 0, t > 0. What is the sign of r(s + t)? Careful -- how many factors are there here?
Inside the parentheses, s + t is positive plus positive. So what sign is that whole quantity, before r touches it?
Two factors: r, which is negative, and (s + t), which is positive. One negative factor, so r(s + t) < 0. Resolve the parenthesis first, then count.

printable_artifact.instructions: Count negatives among FACTORS. Resolve anything inside parentheses to a single sign first.

a < 0, b > 0  ->  ab < 0, whatever a and b are.
r < 0, s > 0, t > 0  ->  (s + t) is POSITIVE, so r(s + t) < 0.

practice_problems.answer: Negative -- exactly one negative factor.

practice_problems.stem: m < 0 and n < 0. Is mn positive or negative?
practice_problems.answer: Positive -- two negative factors.

practice_problems.stem: Suppose a < 0 and b > 0. Which is true about ab: ab > 0, ab < 0, ab = 0, or cannot be determined?
practice_problems.answer: ab < 0
practice_problems.notes: 'Cannot be determined' is the tempting wrong answer -- the sign is fully determined even though the value is not.

practice_problems.stem: If r < 0, s > 0, and t > 0, select the three true statements: (1) rs < 0  (2) rt < 0  (3) r(st) > 0  (4) r(s + t) < 0  (5) r(s + t) > 0  (6) rst = 0
practice_problems.answer: Statements 1, 2, and 4
practice_problems.notes: Statement 5 is the canonical error; statement 3 miscounts a single negative as two; statement 6 invokes the zero-product rule with no zero present.

practice_problems.stem: m < 0 and n < 0. Write an inequality comparing mn to zero, and justify it in one sentence.
practice_problems.answer: mn > 0, because two negative factors make a positive product.

practice_problems.stem: Read Owen's reasoning. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Given: r < 0, s > 0, t > 0. Owen must decide the sign of r(s + t).
Owen wrote: 'r times s is negative. r times t is negative. Two negatives make a positive, so r(s + t) > 0.'
practice_problems.answer: r(s + t) < 0. Owen distributed correctly but then counted rs and rt as FACTORS -- they are being added, not multiplied. Two negative quantities added together make a bigger negative, not a positive. The quick route: s + t is positive plus positive, so it is one positive quantity, and r is one negative factor. One negative factor makes the product negative.
practice_problems.notes: The canonical error. Worth running with numbers too: r = -2, s = 3, t = 4 gives -2(7) = -14, and -6 + -8 = -14. Both routes agree, and neither is positive.

practice_problems.stem: p < 0 and q > 0, and |p| > |q|. What is the sign of p + q? What is the sign of pq? Explain why the two questions need different reasoning.
practice_problems.answer: p + q < 0 and pq < 0. For the sum, the sign depends on which number is farther from zero, so the magnitude fact matters. For the product, only the count of negative factors matters, so |p| > |q| is irrelevant. Sums need magnitude; products need only signs.
practice_problems.notes: Separates the two rules that Owen's error collapses.

practice_problems.stem: Is it possible for a < 0, b < 0, and ab < 0 all to be true at once? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: No. Two negative factors always produce a positive product, so ab < 0 contradicts a < 0 and b < 0. There is no counterexample to find -- the three statements cannot hold together.
practice_problems.notes: Asks students to argue that no case exists, which is harder than producing one.

activities.title: Resolve the Parenthesis First
materials: Folded parenthesis cards holding a sum
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out an expression using sign cards, with one folded card representing a parenthesis holding a sum.
2. Before anyone counts negatives, the group must open the folded card and agree on ONE sign for the whole parenthesis.
3. Replace the folded card with a single sign card carrying that sign.
4. Now count negative factors across the flat layout and name the sign of the product.
5. Repeat with r(s + t), r(s - t) where s < t, and r(st). Ask what changed each time and why.

activities.title: Owen Counted the Wrong Things
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs read Owen's reasoning and mark the exact sentence where it goes wrong.
2. Ask first: why is 'two negatives make a positive' a reasonable thing to reach for? (Because it is true -- for factors.)
3. Pairs test Owen's claim with r = -2, s = 3, t = 4 and report both routes.
4. Pairs write one sentence stating when the two-negatives rule applies and when it does not.

activities.title: Determined or Not
materials: Three response cards per student: POSITIVE, NEGATIVE, DEPENDS
activities.instructions:
1. Post a setup (a < 0, b > 0) and an expression (ab, a + b, a(b + b), ab^2).
2. Students raise a card. DEPENDS is correct only when magnitude decides the answer.
3. Any student showing DEPENDS must produce two cases with different signs; any student showing a sign must state the factor count.
4. Final round: a < 0, b > 0, and |a| > |b| -- ask for a + b and for ab, and let the class find that adding the magnitude fact changes only one of them.

strategy_links.why: Sign claims about letters have no computed answer to check against, so pairs must defend reasoning aloud and meet a counterexample from someone else.

The sign cards and folded parenthesis card give the resolve-then-count order a concrete stage before it becomes symbolic.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4, multiplying signed fractions and decimals, the At-proficiency computational core. If they pass, move up to S5 (distribute a signed factor) and S6 (equivalent signed products). If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks positive fraction multiplication on an area model and B2 checks positive decimal multiplication, the two grade 6 skills that carry the size of every signed product. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (multiplication facts from arrays) and F2 (decimal times whole number) locate the gap in grades 3-5. S1, S2, and S3 remain available to probe the standard's own number-line model, sign rule, and integer products.
